builder_plan.scenario: An agent reads external documents or tool responses that may contain malicious instructions.
builder_plan.change: Replay attacks and legitimate lookalikes in an isolated copy of your agent workflow.
builder_plan.baseline: Your existing checks with the same tasks, permissions, and tool responses.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Successful attacks missed, legitimate actions blocked, detection delay, and review cost.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: How Much Can Tool Calls Reveal About You? Privacy Leakage from Tool-Call Traces
summary: This is not a deployable technique but an attack study: it shows that MCP tool-call traces, even without conversation content, leak user attributes and can substitute for direct access to user data on the attacker's side. For the reader, the cost of the implied mitigation is operational: minimizing logged tool arguments and results, isolating sessions, and restricting trace retention adds engineering complexity and can reduce observability and debugging capability. The main failure mode is assuming conversation-level redaction suffices while tool arguments, returned results, and cross-session linkage continue to expose behavioral signals.
rationale: The paper demonstrates a privacy side channel relevant to anyone deploying MCP-based agents, but it provides no validated defense mechanism to adopt, so the reader should treat it as a threat-model input when logging and retaining tool-call traces.
technique: Profiling attack on MCP tool-call traces

claims.statement: This is not a deployable technique but an attack study: it shows that MCP tool-call traces, even without conversation content, leak user attributes and can substitute for direct access to user data on the attacker's side. For the reader, the cost of the implied mitigation is operational: minimizing logged tool arguments and results, isolating sessions, and restricting trace retention adds engineering complexity and can reduce observability and debugging capability. The main failure mode is assuming conversation-level redaction suffices while tool arguments, returned results, and cross-session linkage continue to expose behavioral signals.
LLM attackers infer user profiles from tool-call traces at a 26.25% success rate versus 17.97% from prior-based guessing; risk increases when traces are linked across sessions.
